title: Word Probability Findings in the Voynich Manuscript
authors: Colin Layfield, Lonneke van der Plas, Michael Rosner, John Abela
summary: The authors compare word probability with segment information and the position at which a word becomes unique among words sharing its beginning. They report relationships in the Voynich transcription resembling those in their natural-language comparisons, while noting that those comparison corpora were generally larger and modern, and that written characters are not phonemic transcriptions.
established: Using the ZL 1b EVA transcription, the study retained 32,216 of 36,249 word tokens after excluding uncertain characters, sequences and spaces; 7,283 retained word types were distinct (section 4.1).

For word lengths four through eight, the manuscript's less frequent word forms had more informative segments on average, in the same direction as the five displayed natural-language comparisons (section 5 and figure 2). The information calculation removes the word's own count from its segment counts.

The authors report significantly earlier relative uniqueness points for less probable manuscript words across the tested word lengths (section 5 and figure 3). A uniqueness point is the first prefix that identifies a word among the retained word types.

open.question: Do the reported relationships between word probability, segment information and relative uniqueness-point position persist when compared with written corpora of similar size from roughly the manuscript's period?
open.check: Reproduce the paper's word-length-stratified measures on the public transcription and size-matched historical corpora, then compare the same prespecified relationships on hidden manuscript pages.
